---
title: "Comparing one-cycle videos"
subtitle: "The same 106 recordings folded twice — once on the FIR band-pass phase, once on the M-SSA phase — 10 bins, one averaged cardiac cycle, and a shuffled phase to tell us what any of it is worth"
include-in-header: figures_one_cycle_compare/plotlyjs.html
---

The [previous page](data-pulse-extraction-methods.qmd) compared seven ways of
getting a cardiac **phase** out of a registered B-scan video, and ranked them by
how well each agreed with the FIR band-pass. That ranking presupposed its own
answer: it scored every method against FIR, so FIR could not lose.

This page asks the question the pipeline actually needs answered. The phase is
never the deliverable either — the **folded video** is, and the choroidal
thickness curve read off it. So take the two most distinct methods from that
page, fold the video with each, and judge the *result*.

Nothing here is recomputed. The pulses and the phases are read straight out of
the `.npz` files the previous page's batch script wrote. The two folds get the
same frames, the same uniform time grid, the same 10 bins, the same median
folding and the same set of retained frames. **Only the phase differs**, so every
difference below is attributable to the phase and to nothing else.

{{< include figures_one_cycle_compare/tab_cohort.qmd >}}

## The one thing that makes these numbers readable

A folded video always looks plausible. Average forty B-scans into each of ten
bins and you get ten clean B-scans, whatever phase you used to sort them — so
"the video looks good" is not evidence of anything.

Every measurement on this page is therefore run a third time on a **shuffled
phase**: the FIR phase, randomly permuted over the uniform grid, carried through
the identical resampling and folding. Same frames, same bins, same everything —
no timing. It is the only scale these numbers have, and it turns out to be a
demanding one.

Three quantities are measured, all of them on both real phases and on the null:

- **split-half reproducibility** — the first half of the recording and the second
  are folded separately and the two cycles correlated, after removing each one's
  temporal mean so that the static anatomy (identical either way, and enough on
  its own to push any correlation towards 1) cannot contribute. A phase that
  tracks the heartbeat gives the same cycle twice; a phase that does not gives
  two independent noises. Measured on three representations of the same cycle —
  per pixel, on the column-averaged depth profile, and on the thickness curve —
  because they have very different signal-to-noise, and only their agreement is
  worth reading.
- **ΔY** — peak-to-peak of the folded thickness curve, obtained by folding the
  *masks* with the same phase. This is the quantity the rigidity coefficient is
  built on.
- **bin occupancy** — how evenly the ten bins fill.

## One condition, two phases

{{< include figures_one_cycle_compare/f1_thickness_ref.qmd >}}

Solid lines are the whole recording; dotted lines are each half folded on its
own. The gap between a method's two dotted curves is its split-half error, drawn
rather than summarised — and on this condition, which is a perfectly ordinary
one, that gap is comparable to the amplitude of the curve itself.

{{< include figures_one_cycle_compare/f2_bins_ref.qmd >}}

Bin occupancy is close to uniform for both, which is what a phase that advances
at a roughly constant rate produces. It is a sanity check, not a discriminator:
the shuffled null fills the bins evenly too, by construction.

## The two phases are not the same phase

{{< include figures_one_cycle_compare/f3_phase_agreement.qmd >}}

This is the first substantive result, and it is larger than expected.

The two phases sit within 30° of each other — under a twelfth of a cycle — in
**66 of 106 conditions**. In **30** they are more than a quarter-cycle apart, and
in **18** more than 150° apart. Nine of those eighteen hold that near-inversion
with a phase-locking value above 0.5: a *stable* half-cycle offset, not
jitter. For those recordings the two videos are the same cycle played half a
period out of step — one shows the choroid filling where the other shows it
emptying.

The phase-locking value, which measures whether the offset at least stays
constant, has a median of **0.59**, and **83 of 106** conditions fall below 0.9.
The two folded cycles correlate at a median of **0.15**, and **73 of 106** below
0.3. Read plainly: on most of this cohort, the two methods do not produce
variants of one video. They produce two different videos.

## Does either phase beat a shuffled one?

{{< include figures_one_cycle_compare/f4_split_half_null.qmd >}}

Both do — significantly, and by very little.

Against its own per-condition null (Wilcoxon signed-rank over the 106 paired
differences), the FIR phase is ahead on the thickness curve ($p = 5\times10^{-4}$)
and on ΔY ($p = 0.005$), marginal per pixel ($p = 0.049$) and not significant on
the depth profile ($p = 0.08$). M-SSA is ahead on all four: per pixel
($p = 7\times10^{-5}$), depth profile ($p = 0.01$), thickness curve
($p = 0.002$), ΔY ($p = 3\times10^{-4}$).

So there is real cardiac timing in both phases — the folding is not an
elaborate way of averaging noise. But look at the absolute values in the table
below rather than the $p$-values. The median split-half correlation is **0.11**
(FIR) and **0.15** (M-SSA) on the thickness curve, against **−0.03** for the
shuffled phase. A cycle that reproduced across halves would sit near 1. These
sit near zero, and they clear the null by a margin that takes 106 conditions to
establish.

{{< include figures_one_cycle_compare/tab_methods.qmd >}}

One row of that table deserves to be read as a warning rather than a result.
**Modulation depth is identical for all three columns** — 0.029, 0.030, 0.030 —
including the shuffled phase. The intensity modulation left in a folded cycle is
entirely explained by having averaged a finite number of frames per bin. It
measures the bin count, not the heartbeat, and it should not be used to judge a
fold. It is kept here precisely to say so.

## FIR against M-SSA

{{< include figures_one_cycle_compare/f4b_split_half_paired.qmd >}}

Head to head, the honest answer is **M-SSA is at least as good, and better where
the test has the most power**:

| measured on | FIR ahead in | Wilcoxon $p$ |
|:--|--:|--:|
| per pixel (~10⁶ points) | 35 % of conditions | 0.003 (favours M-SSA) |
| depth profile | 46 % | 0.19 |
| thickness curve (10 points) | 52 % | 0.87 |
| ΔY | 42 % | 0.051 |

The per-pixel test is the one with the sample size to resolve a small effect,
and it favours M-SSA. The two reduced representations cannot separate them.
Nothing here supports preferring FIR.

That is the opposite of the previous page's ranking, and the reason is
methodological rather than empirical. There, M-SSA scored 0.54 against a
reference *defined* as the FIR pulse; a method that departs from FIR is
penalised whether it departs towards the truth or away from it. Judged on the
folded video against a null instead, the departure looks like the better cycle.
M-SSA's flattening of beat-to-beat amplitude modulation — the property that
counted against it before — costs it nothing here, because folding discards
amplitude and keeps only timing.

## What this costs downstream

{{< include figures_one_cycle_compare/f5_deltaY.qmd >}}

This is the figure to worry about, and it is the bluntest result on the page.
Read as **peak-to-peak of the folded thickness curve — the raw max minus min
over the ten bins — ΔY does not beat the shuffled phase at all**:

| | FIR band-pass | M-SSA | shuffled (null) |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| median ΔY peak-to-peak (px) | 1.81 | 1.91 | **2.19** |
| beats its own null in | 51 % of conditions | 60 % | — |
| Wilcoxon $p$ vs null | 0.84 | 0.23 | — |

The null is not merely close, it is **nominally the largest of the three**, and
neither real phase is significantly above it. In **49 % of conditions the FIR
fold returns less peak-to-peak ΔY than that condition's own shuffled phase** — a
coin flip.

The reason is that peak-to-peak is an extreme-value statistic. Max-minus-min over
ten noisy bins grows with the noise, so a phase that scatters frames at random
inflates it just as effectively as a phase that sorts them correctly — sometimes
more so, since a correct sort averages coherently and *reduces* per-bin variance.
Peak-to-peak ΔY therefore measures frames-per-bin at least as much as it measures
the choroid, in the same way modulation depth did above.

The signal is not absent; it only survives once the curve is reduced to its
fundamental. Fitting one harmonic to the same ten points before taking the
amplitude — the `ΔY, 1-harmonic fit` row of the methods table — gives 0.86 px
(FIR) and 1.04 px (M-SSA) against 0.70 px for the null, and *both* clear it
significantly ($p = 0.005$ and $p = 3\times10^{-4}$). Same data, same folds; the
difference is entirely in whether the amplitude is read from two extreme bins or
from all ten.

The practical consequence for the rigidity coefficient is direct: **ΔY should be
taken from a harmonic fit of the folded curve, never from its peak-to-peak
range.** Beyond that, the two things that would raise the floor are neither a
change of phase method nor a change of estimator — more frames per bin (longer
recordings, or fewer bins), and a thickness measurement less sensitive to
per-frame mask jitter than summing a folded binary mask.

{{< include figures_one_cycle_compare/f6_bin_uniformity.qmd >}}

{{< include figures_one_cycle_compare/f7_disagreement_cost.qmd >}}

Where the two phases disagree most — low phase-locking value, on the left — the
split-half gain of one over the other scatters symmetrically about zero. The
disagreement does not resolve in favour of either method; it is simply where
both are least determined.

## All 106 one-cycle videos

Every condition has its own page, carrying three things: the comparison video
(FIR on top, M-SSA below, both folded from the same frames); **ΔY along the
folded cycle**, with the shuffled null superimposed on the two real phases; and
**the two pulses overlaid, their phase, and the instantaneous heart rate** on the
full recording, which is where a phase that loses the beat becomes visible.

The ΔY columns below are peak-to-peak, with the null beside them — on a good
many rows the null is the largest of the three, which is the cohort result of the
previous section seen one condition at a time.

{{< include figures_one_cycle_compare/_table.qmd >}}

## Conclusion

- **The two phases do not fold the same video.** Median correlation between the
  two folded cycles is 0.15; in 18 conditions of 106 they are more than 150°
  apart, nine of them stably so — half a cardiac cycle, systole read as diastole.
- **Both phases beat a shuffled phase, and both beat it narrowly.** Median
  split-half reproducibility of 0.11 (FIR) and 0.15 (M-SSA) against −0.03 for the
  null. The timing is real; the folded cycle is not yet reproducible.
- **M-SSA is not worse than the FIR band-pass for folding, and is better on the
  most powerful test** ($p = 0.003$ per pixel). The previous page's ranking
  measured agreement with FIR, which is a different question from correctness,
  and it should not be carried over to this one.
- **The ΔY noise floor is the binding constraint**, not the choice of phase
  method — and how ΔY is read off the folded curve decides whether there is any
  signal at all. **Peak-to-peak does not beat a shuffled phase** (1.81 / 1.91 px
  against 2.19 px for the null, $p = 0.84$ and $0.23$); a 1-harmonic fit of the
  same ten points does (0.86 / 1.04 against 0.70 px, $p = 0.005$ and
  $3\times10^{-4}$). Use the fit.
- **Two of the obvious quality metrics measure the bin count, not the
  heartbeat** — modulation depth and peak-to-peak ΔY are both matched or beaten
  by a shuffled phase. Any metric proposed for this pipeline should be run
  against the null before it is trusted.

::: {.source-note}
Videos and tables produced by `Astronauts/compute_one_cycle_compare_methods.py`
(106 conditions, masks `model1_scale_1.0`, 10 bins, one averaged cycle, median
folding, one cardiac cycle trimmed at each end of the record for both methods
alike). Pulses and phases are read from
`pulse_from_data/traces/<slug>.npz` and never re-estimated. Figures, per-condition
pages and the link table are generated by
`figures_one_cycle_compare/make_figures.py`, which only reads the three CSVs, the
per-condition `.npz` and the videos. Everything lives under `E:/NASA_Rigidity/`.
Re-run the figure script rather than editing the generated fragments (`f*.qmd`,
`tab_*.qmd`, `_table.qmd`, `one_cycles/oc_*.qmd`) by hand. The per-condition
pages plot their thickness curves as inline SVG rather than Plotly: `plotly.js`
is 4.9 MB and `include-in-header` inlines it per page, so 106 interactive
sparklines would cost half a gigabyte. The figures on this page are interactive.
:::
